title: Tag questions e fillers
theme: Tag questions sistemáticas (to be, do/does/did, have, modais, casos especiais) + fillers conversacionais (you know, I mean, like, well)
goal: Student forms tag questions correctly across tenses and modals, and uses conversational fillers naturally without sounding hesitant.
connects_to: A09 (idioms gerais) e A21 (native fluency) — extends conversational naturalness into Advanced.
module_chunks: I am right, aren't I? (special case)
Kind of / Sort of / Pretty much
I guess... / I suppose... / I'd say...

units.title: Tags com to be e have
units.grammar_focus: Tag questions with "to be" (present and past) and "have/has/had"
units.real_life_context: You confirm information or invite agreement using tag questions with the most common auxiliaries.

grammar.explanation: Positive statement with "is" → negative tag "isn't she?". Tag questions reverse polarity. Positive statement + negative tag, or negative statement + positive tag. Auxiliary matches the verb in the main clause.
Negative statement "aren't" → positive tag "are you?". Reverse polarity rule. Match the auxiliary (in this case, the "be" verb) to the original.

grammar.sentence: They were at the meeting, _____ they?
grammar.explanation: Past tense "were" → past tense negative tag "weren't they?". Match tense and verb form. "Wasn't" would be singular (she/he/it).

grammar.sentence: He has finished the project, _____ he?
grammar.explanation: Present perfect "has" → negative tag "hasn't he?". When "have" is the auxiliary in the main clause, use "have/has" in the tag too.
"We've" = "we have" → negative tag "haven't we?". Always match the contracted auxiliary in the statement.
"It's a beautiful day, isn't it?" — extremely common conversational tag. Almost a fixed greeting/observation pattern in English.

grammar.sentence: She wasn't at the party, _____ she?
grammar.explanation: Negative "wasn't" → positive tag "was she?". Reverse polarity. The tag asks if the negative is true, expecting yes/no confirmation.
Tag verb must match the main verb. "Are" → "aren't" for negative tag, not "isn't". "Isn't" is the negative of "is" (third person singular).

grammar.sentence: He has been working hard, isn't he?
grammar.answer: He has been working hard, hasn't he?
grammar.explanation: When the main verb is "has been + -ing" (present perfect continuous), the tag uses the auxiliary "has" → "hasn't he?". "Isn't" doesn't fit because "is" isn't the auxiliary here.

grammar.passage: You're new here, aren't you? I haven't seen you before. She's the new manager, isn't she? And they were just hired last week, weren't they? Everyone's still learning each other's names.
grammar.question: How many tag questions are in the passage?
grammar.answer: three (aren't you, isn't she, weren't they) — or four if "haven't seen" counted, though that isn't a tag
grammar.explanation: Three tag questions: "aren't you?", "isn't she?", "weren't they?". Each reverses polarity from positive to negative. The passage uses tags for social warmth — opening conversation, confirming knowledge.

listening_speaking.text: She's been busy lately, hasn't she?
They weren't at the meeting, were they?
You haven't met him before, have you?

units.title: Tags com do/does/did
units.grammar_focus: Tag questions with "do/does/did" — for simple present and simple past with main verbs (not auxiliaries)
units.real_life_context: You form tags when the main verb is a regular action verb (no "be", no "have", no modal).

grammar.explanation: Main verb is "like" (no auxiliary visible) → tag uses "do/does". "You like" is present simple, second person → "don't you?". Always add "do" support for action verbs without "be" or modal.
"She works" (third person singular present simple) → "doesn't she?". "Works" implies "does work", so the tag uses "doesn't".

grammar.sentence: They went to the concert, _____ they?
grammar.explanation: "Went" is past simple → tag uses "did/didn't". Past simple action verb → "didn't they?". "Weren't" would only fit if the main verb were "were".
Negative "doesn't speak" → positive tag "does he?". Reverse polarity rule applies to "do/does/did" too.
"Didn't see" (negative) → positive tag "did you?". Reverse polarity. Common when confirming someone wasn't seen or didn't happen.
"Speaks" (present simple third person) → "doesn't she?". Reminder: the third person "s" disappears in the tag because "doesn't" carries it.

grammar.sentence: They lived in Paris last year, _____ they?
grammar.explanation: "Lived" (past simple) → "didn't they?". Past tense in main clause requires "did/didn't" in tag.
Tag must match the auxiliary that would be used in negation/question of the main verb. "You like" → "Do you like?" / "You don't like" → so tag is "don't you?". "Aren't" doesn't fit "like".
"He drinks" is third person singular → auxiliary "does/doesn't". "Don't" is only for I/you/we/they. Common error: forgetting third person -s in the tag.

grammar.passage: You go to the gym every morning, don't you? I see you there sometimes. She works out too, doesn't she? Last week they were both there at 6am, weren't they? You all wake up so early — I don't know how you do it.
grammar.question: Which tag question uses "don't"?
grammar.answer: "you go to the gym every morning, don't you?"
grammar.explanation: The passage uses three different tag formations: "don't you?" (for "you go"), "doesn't she?" (for "she works out"), "weren't they?" (for "they were"). Each tag matches the verb form in the main clause.

listening_speaking.text: They went home early, didn't they?

units.title: Tags com modais
units.grammar_focus: Tag questions with modals (can, could, will, would, should, must)
units.real_life_context: You confirm abilities, possibilities, and obligations using modal-based tag questions.

grammar.explanation: Modal "can" → negative tag "can't you?". With modals, the tag uses the same modal. No "do/does" needed since modals are auxiliaries themselves.
"Will" (contracted in "she'll") → negative tag "won't she?". Future modal "will" pairs with "won't" in negative tag.
Modal "should" → negative tag "shouldn't we?". Same modal echoes in the tag with negation.
Negative "couldn't" → positive tag "could he?". Modal stays the same; polarity reverses.

grammar.sentence: You wouldn't lie to me, _____ you?
grammar.explanation: "Wouldn't" → "would you?". Conditional modal "would" in positive tag.

grammar.hint: "Must" usually pairs with "mustn't" in tag, though "must" often gets a different tag in real speech
grammar.explanation: "Must" technically pairs with "mustn't" in textbook tags. In real speech, "She must be tired, isn't she?" is more common when "must" expresses certainty rather than obligation.
"Can you?" / "Can't you?" — "can" tag forms regularly. Note: in tag, "can't" never spelled "cant".

grammar.sentence: You should call her, don't you?
grammar.answer: You should call her, shouldn't you?
grammar.explanation: Modal "should" pairs with "shouldn't" in negative tag. "Don't" only works for action verbs without modals. Mistake comes from forgetting that "should" is an auxiliary itself.

grammar.sentence: He can play guitar, can he?
grammar.hint: Positive statement needs negative tag — "can't he?"
grammar.answer: He can play guitar, can't he?
grammar.explanation: Positive statement "can play" requires negative tag "can't he?". The tag with "can he?" would only be correct after a negative statement like "He can't play guitar, can he?".

grammar.passage: We should leave by eight, shouldn't we? Traffic gets terrible after that. You'll be ready, won't you? Marco can drive us, can't he? It would be faster than the train, wouldn't it?
grammar.question: Which modal appears most often?
grammar.answer: "would" (in "wouldn't it?" and implied), or "will/should/can" each once
grammar.explanation: The passage uses modal tags: "shouldn't we?", "won't you?", "can't he?", "wouldn't it?". Each tag echoes the modal of the main clause with negation. The structure is uniform across different modals.

units.title: Casos especiais
units.grammar_focus: Special tag cases — "I am → aren't I", "Let's → shall we", imperative tags (will you?), tags with indefinite subjects (everyone, nobody, somebody)
units.real_life_context: You handle the tricky exceptions to the basic tag question rules — common cases that don't follow the standard pattern.

grammar.explanation: Special case: "I am" → tag uses "aren't I?". Logically should be "amn't I?" (which exists in Scottish/Irish dialects) but standard English uses "aren't I?" to avoid the awkward "amn't". One of the strangest exceptions in English grammar.

grammar.sentence: Let's go to the park, _____ we?
grammar.explanation: Special case: "Let's" → tag is "shall we?". Sounds slightly formal but it's the correct form. "Let's" is suggestion + invitation, and "shall we?" extends the invitation. Don't use "do we?" or "don't we?".
Imperative + tag: "Open the door, will you?" — softens a command into a polite request. Variations: "would you?", "could you?", "won't you?". All make the imperative friendlier.

Special case: with indefinite subjects (nobody, no one, none) the tag uses plural "they" and reversed polarity. "Nobody called" (negative meaning) → positive tag "did they?". The pronoun shift to "they" handles the gender-neutral reference.

"Aren't I?" — the standard English solution to the missing negative of "I am". "Amn't" exists in some dialects but isn't standard. C2 awareness: this is one of the few cases where "are" pairs with "I".
"Let's + verb" pairs with "shall we?" tag. Fixed pattern, even though "shall" is otherwise rare in American English. Used for suggestions/invitations.

"Everyone" takes a singular verb ("enjoys") but the tag uses plural "they" — "don't they?". This avoids gender-specific "he/she" while staying natural. Common pattern with everyone/somebody/anyone/nobody.

grammar.sentence: I am wrong, am I not?
grammar.explanation: "Am I not?" is grammatically logical but extremely formal/old-fashioned. Standard modern English uses "aren't I?" as the accepted irregular tag for "I am". C2 awareness of register.
"Let's" is a contraction of "let us" (a suggestion), and its tag is "shall we?". Using "will we?" sounds wrong because "shall" carries the suggestive force. Fixed exception.

grammar.passage: I am late, aren't I? Sorry. Let's order food, shall we? You don't mind if I pay later, do you? Nobody else is coming, are they? Open the window, would you? It's stuffy in here.
grammar.question: Which two tags are special exceptions to the standard rule?
grammar.answer: "aren't I?" (special tag for "I am") and "shall we?" (special tag for "let's"). Also "are they?" (for "nobody") and "would you?" (after imperative).
grammar.explanation: The passage strings together multiple special cases: "aren't I?" (irregular for "I am"), "shall we?" (for "let's"), "are they?" (indefinite subject "nobody"), "would you?" (softening imperative). All exceptions to the basic positive-negative rule.

units.title: Fillers naturais
units.grammar_focus: Conversational fillers (you know, I mean, like, well, so, right) used naturally — plus rising vs falling intonation distinction in tag questions
units.real_life_context: You add fillers strategically to sound natural and confident — not nervous. You also know when a tag is a real question (rising) vs rhetorical (falling).

grammar.explanation: "I mean..." — filler used to clarify, correct, or emphasize what you really mean. Different from "like" (pause/example), "well" (hesitation start), or "so" (transition/conclusion). Each filler has its own pragmatic role.
"Well..." — natural opening filler signaling you're about to start an answer. Buys thinking time without sounding hesitant. "Right" confirms; "actually" corrects; "obviously" makes a claim.

grammar.sentence: _____ , I haven't really thought about it.
grammar.explanation: "Well" introduces a hesitant or thoughtful answer. Natural conversational opener that signals reflection rather than uncertainty.
"Kind of" (or "sort of") — softener filler meaning "more or less" / "somewhat". Hedges the strength of the claim. Common in casual speech to avoid sounding too definitive.
"Like" — pause filler especially common in younger speech. Signals you're searching, processing, or about to give an example. Overuse sounds immature but moderate use is natural.

grammar.hint: tag with rising intonation expecting confirmation
grammar.explanation: "Isn't she?" with rising intonation = genuine question seeking confirmation. The speaker isn't sure and wants the listener to confirm or deny. Different from rhetorical use.

grammar.hint: same tag form but with falling intonation
grammar.explanation: "Isn't it?" with falling intonation = rhetorical statement seeking agreement, not info. The speaker assumes agreement. Same tag form; intonation carries the function.

grammar.sentence: I, like, you know, I mean, kind of, well, don't really know.
grammar.hint: Too many fillers — sound nervous; pick one or two
grammar.explanation: Stacking fillers makes you sound nervous and uncertain. Use one or two naturally. C2 fluency is about strategic placement, not quantity. Excess fillers undermine confidence.

grammar.sentence: Obviously you don't know what I'm talking about.
grammar.hint: "Obviously" can sound condescending — use "I mean" or rephrase
grammar.answer: I mean, you might not know what I'm talking about. (or simply: "Maybe you don't know what I'm talking about.")
grammar.explanation: "Obviously" implies the listener should know — can sound condescending. In sensitive conversations, "I mean" or "actually" is softer. Register awareness is part of using fillers well.

grammar.passage: Well, I think — I mean, you know how it is — sometimes you just need a break. Kind of. So I told my boss I needed a few days. She was, like, totally understanding. It's a good company to work for, isn't it?
grammar.question: How many different fillers appear in the passage?
grammar.answer: at least six — "Well", "I mean", "you know", "Kind of", "So", "like"
grammar.explanation: The passage uses many fillers naturally: "Well" (opener), "I mean" (clarification), "you know" (shared understanding), "Kind of" (hedge), "So" (transition), "like" (pause/example). Combined sparingly, they create natural conversational rhythm. "Isn't it?" at the end is a tag, not a filler.

You know, that's a good question.

cross_unit_consolidation: Form tag questions with "to be" and "have" (isn't / aren't / wasn't / haven't / hasn't)
Form tag questions with "do/does/did" for action verbs without auxiliaries
Form tag questions with all common modals (can/can't, will/won't, should/shouldn't, would/wouldn't)
Handle special cases: "I am → aren't I", "Let's → shall we", imperative + "will you?", indefinite subjects + "they"
Use conversational fillers (well, I mean, you know, like, kind of, sort of) strategically — not nervously
Distinguish rising vs falling intonation in tag questions (genuine question vs rhetorical)
Sound conversationally natural without overusing fillers
